title: Week 27 · Lesson 51: Emergency & Urgent Care Pharmacology — Anaphylaxis, Asthma, ACS, Sepsis & Medication Safety
html:
PHASE 2 · ADVANCED PHARMACOLOGY

Week 27 — Lesson 51: Emergency & Urgent Care Pharmacology — Anaphylaxis, Asthma, ACS, Sepsis & Medication Safety

FNP-level goal: Recognize when time-critical medication and emergency disposition are both required. In urgent care, the right drug does not replace airway assessment, serial vital signs, EMS activation, emergency transfer, or clear handoff.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify anaphylaxis and explain why epinephrine is the first-line medication for suspected anaphylaxis.
  • Differentiate an asthma exacerbation needing escalation from a routine rescue-medication refill.
  • Recognize acute coronary syndrome symptoms and prioritize emergency transport over outpatient treatment.
  • Apply early recognition and immediate escalation principles for sepsis and shock.
  • Use a medication-safety approach for urgent care: allergies, contraindications, monitoring, transfer, and handoff.

Part 1 — Urgent-Care Pharmacology Begins With ABCs and Disposition

Medication choice in an emergency is inseparable from airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, perfusion, and serial vital signs. A patient who is hypoxic, hypotensive, confused, cyanotic, severely dyspneic, actively bleeding, or deteriorating needs a higher level of care even when an initial medication has been given.

FNP clinical reasoning: stabilize within scope, call for help early, activate EMS/transfer when indicated, document time and response, and give a concise handoff. Do not let task focus—such as finding an antibiotic, inhaler, or EKG interpretation—delay emergency disposition.

Part 2 — Anaphylaxis Is a Multi-System Emergency

Anaphylaxis is a rapidly developing systemic allergic reaction that can involve airway swelling, wheeze/bronchospasm, respiratory compromise, hypotension, syncope, severe GI symptoms, skin/mucosal findings, or a known exposure plus a concerning pattern. Skin findings may be absent. Do not wait for hives before acting when airway, breathing, or circulation is involved.

Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line treatment for suspected anaphylaxis. Antihistamines may address skin symptoms but do not reverse airway edema, bronchospasm, or shock and must not delay epinephrine. Bronchodilators are adjuncts for lower-airway bronchospasm, not replacements for epinephrine in anaphylaxis.

Part 3 — Anaphylaxis: Medication Plus Monitoring

After epinephrine, reassess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and response; prepare for repeat treatment and emergency transfer according to current protocol and patient response. Severe, persistent, recurrent, or incompletely resolving symptoms require EMS/emergency care. Observe and counsel for recurrence risk according to current guidance.

Before discharge from a non-emergency setting, a patient needs an individualized action plan, education on correct auto-injector use when indicated, access to medication, avoidance counseling, and appropriate allergy follow-up. “Symptoms improved” is not the same as “the patient is safe without a plan.”

Part 4 — Asthma Exacerbation: Treat Severity, Not Just Wheeze

Assess speech, work of breathing, respiratory rate, oxygenation, mental status, accessory-muscle use, hydration, peak flow when appropriate, prior ICU/intubation history, rescue-medication use, trigger, and response to initial treatment. A quiet chest, exhaustion, altered mental status, hypoxemia, cyanosis, or worsening after initial therapy can indicate impending respiratory failure—not improvement.

Short-acting bronchodilator therapy is used for acute bronchoconstriction. Systemic anti-inflammatory therapy may be appropriate in selected moderate/severe exacerbations under current guidelines. Long-term controller therapy and inhaler technique must be reviewed after stabilization. Do not send a patient home simply because a few wheezes improved if the overall severity or safety context remains concerning.

Part 5 — Epi, Albuterol, and “Response to Treatment”

In emergency care, response to medication must be measured, not assumed. Reassess vital signs, oxygenation, work of breathing, lung examination, mental status, and function after treatment. Tachycardia or tremor may occur with bronchodilator therapy, but new chest pain, hypotension, poor perfusion, or clinical deterioration requires reconsideration of the diagnosis and level of care.

Do not anchor on asthma if the patient has chest pain, unilateral absent breath sounds, stridor, swelling, fever/toxic appearance, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism risk, or anaphylaxis signs. Similar symptoms can arise from very different emergencies.

Part 6 — Acute Coronary Syndrome: Activate EMS

ACS can present with chest pressure, pain/discomfort, dyspnea, diaphoresis, nausea, lightheadedness, weakness, or discomfort in the jaw, neck, back, epigastrium, arm, or shoulder. Older adults, women, and people with diabetes may have less typical presentations. A normal-looking patient or a temporarily improved symptom does not rule out ACS.

For suspected ACS, emergency response/EMS transport is the priority. Do not ask a patient to drive, wait for a family member, or “see if it goes away.” Aspirin may be appropriate in selected alert patients without allergy, bleeding concern, or other contraindication under emergency guidance, but it must never delay EMS activation or be used as a diagnostic test.

Part 7 — Nitrates and PDE5 Medication Safety

Nitrates can be part of an established angina/ACS protocol for appropriate patients, but they are not universally safe. Reconcile recent PDE5 inhibitor exposure, blood pressure, right-ventricular infarction concern, other vasodilators, and the patient’s prescribed plan. The PDE5-nitrate interaction can cause dangerous hypotension.

Ask explicitly about erectile-dysfunction medication, topical nitrate use, PRN nitroglycerin, and “chest-pain pills.” A patient may not volunteer these medications unless asked directly. In unstable chest pain, the transfer and handoff are more important than improvising an outpatient medication plan.

Part 8 — Sepsis: Infection Plus Organ Dysfunction Risk

Sepsis is a life-threatening dysregulated response to infection with organ dysfunction risk. Fever may be absent, especially in older or immunocompromised patients. Concerning findings include hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypoxia, mottled/cool skin, reduced urine output, severe weakness, or rapidly deteriorating appearance.

Suspected sepsis requires immediate assessment, resuscitation/transfer pathways, diagnostics, source evaluation, and timely antimicrobial therapy in the appropriate emergency setting. Do not delay transfer to complete an exhaustive outpatient workup. Antibiotic choice and timing must follow current local/emergency protocols, likely source, allergy history, organ function, cultures when feasible without harmful delay, and severity.

Part 9 — Shock: The Medication Does Not Fix the Cause Alone

Shock can be hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive, or mixed. Hypotension is a late finding in some patients. Look for altered mental status, poor urine output, weak pulses, cool or mottled skin, prolonged capillary refill, rising lactate when available, or severe respiratory distress.

Fluids, vasopressors, bronchodilators, epinephrine, antibiotics, blood products, or anticoagulation may be appropriate in different contexts—but wrong therapy can harm. Identify likely mechanism, use emergency protocols, and transfer. The FNP role is not to deliver prolonged definitive resuscitation in an outpatient room without appropriate resources.

Part 10 — Medication Allergy Versus Adverse Effect

In urgent care, an “allergy” label can change antimicrobial, analgesic, and emergency-medication decisions. Clarify agent, reaction, timing, severity, treatment needed, and subsequent tolerance when time and patient stability permit. A remote GI upset and anaphylaxis are not equivalent labels.

However, an unstable patient comes first. Do not delay life-saving treatment to perform a detailed historical review when the emergency algorithm requires action. Document and communicate uncertainty clearly during transfer.

Part 11 — Clinical Case: Food Exposure and Breathing Difficulty

A patient with a known food allergy develops diffuse hives, throat tightness, wheeze, vomiting, and dizziness shortly after a restaurant meal. They ask for diphenhydramine.

FNP reasoning: multi-system symptoms after likely allergen exposure suggest anaphylaxis. Epinephrine is first line; antihistamine is not a substitute. Activate the emergency pathway, reassess continuously, and arrange appropriate emergency care and handoff.

Part 12 — Clinical Case: “Just an Inhaler Refill”

A patient with asthma has used a rescue inhaler repeatedly since last night and is now speaking in short phrases with visible retractions.

FNP reasoning: this is an acute severity/disposition problem. Start immediate protocol-appropriate care within scope, monitor response, and arrange emergency transfer. A refill or routine telehealth plan is unsafe.

Part 13 — Clinical Case: Indigestion in a High-Risk Patient

A 66-year-old with diabetes reports epigastric pressure, sweating, nausea, and new dyspnea. They believe it is reflux.

FNP reasoning: treat ACS as a possibility. Activate EMS, obtain available emergency assessment without delaying transport, reconcile contraindications before any medication, and provide a focused handoff. Do not try an antacid and wait for relief.

Part 14 — Clinical Case: Infection and Confusion

An older adult with recent UTI symptoms is now febrile, confused, hypotensive, and has decreased urine output.

FNP reasoning: this is possible sepsis with organ dysfunction. Activate emergency transfer/resuscitation pathway immediately; outpatient oral antibiotics and delayed follow-up are insufficient.

FNP Emergency & Urgent-Care Medication Framework

  1. Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, vital signs, and immediate instability first.
  2. Identify the emergency syndrome and activate EMS/transfer early when indicated.
  3. Give time-critical medication according to current protocol, known contraindications, and patient response.
  4. Reassess after every intervention; document time, dose, response, and deterioration.
  5. Do not use adjunct medication to delay first-line treatment or transfer.
  6. Provide a concise handoff: timeline, symptoms, vital signs, allergies, medications, treatments, response, and clinical concern.

High-Yield Summary

Anaphylaxis: epinephrine is first line; antihistamines and bronchodilators are adjuncts, not substitutes.
Asthma: assess work of breathing and function; exhaustion, hypoxemia, altered mental status, or poor response needs escalation.
ACS: activate EMS for suspected symptoms; aspirin may be appropriate only when not contraindicated and must not delay transport.
Nitrates: reconcile PDE5 exposure and hemodynamic context.
Sepsis/shock: deterioration, poor perfusion, hypotension, confusion, and low urine output require immediate emergency pathway.
Urgent care: medication, monitoring, transfer, and handoff are one safety process.

Clinical safety note: This lesson is educational. Emergency medication selection, dosing, monitoring, resuscitation, transfer, and disposition must follow current emergency protocols, FDA-approved prescribing information, local scope requirements, and the individual patient’s clinical context.
